title: Space Weapons: Ask Where They Are First
part1:
When reading news about space weapons, you can get lost if you open the list of specifications right away. The first thing to ask is not what they can hit, but where they are. Are they on the ground, or in orbit? This difference in address divides the issue in a major way.

On September 14, 2026, the U.S. Secretary of the Air Force said that the United States had deployed space-control weapons in orbit to protect the joint force from the actions of hostile parties. An official U.S. government article records this as the first statement to acknowledge that the U.S. Space Force had deployed weapons in space.

But do not try to play detective here. The specific system name is not known. Its attack abilities and targets have not been confirmed. Just seeing the name “space-control weapons” is not enough to decide that they are anti-satellite weapons.
part2:
Russia’s example shows us the difference in address. On November 15, 2021, Russia launched a direct-ascent anti-satellite missile from the ground and destroyed the satellite Kosmos 1408. The amount of trackable space debris exceeded 1,500 pieces. This was a test in which a weapon on the ground was sent into space to attack a satellite. Its address is different from permanently keeping the weapon itself in orbit.

So, what is counterspace? This term does not refer only to weapons placed in space. In the U.S. Space Force’s framework, it includes orbits, communication links, and attacks and defenses carried out on the ground. It may also include actions such as using electromagnetic attacks to interfere with communications or cyberattacks to disrupt satellite networks. Even without destroying a satellite, an action can still be counterspace.
part3:
Tools used for defense should not all be put on the same shelf. Warning about threats, making satellites harder to damage, spreading out their functions, and keeping backups are all examples. These kinds of passive defense are different from attack weapons in orbit. Sensor satellites that warn of and track missiles are also not the same as attack weapons. However, active defense can include weapons, too, so names alone cannot sort everything perfectly.

Finally, there is the treaty. The Outer Space Treaty bans putting nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction into orbit around Earth, or placing them on celestial bodies such as the Moon. It also does not permit military bases or weapons tests on celestial bodies. However, it cannot be read as a treaty that bans putting all conventional weapons into orbit.

Now that satellite communications and positioning have become part of daily life, space weapons news cannot be understood from specifications alone. First look at the address, then the role, and finally check the legal shelf. Space security is less a weapons catalog than a somewhat complicated address book.
in_one_line: To understand space weapons, first ask whether they are on the ground or in orbit, not what they can do.
